content: Northern Colletes is a species of bee that belongs to the genus Colletes. These bees are solitary in nature, meaning they do not form colonies like social bees. However, female Northern Colletes may nest in close proximity to one another in what are referred to as aggregations. These aggregations involve bees nesting near each other without exhibiting the cooperative behaviors seen in social bee colonies. Their nests are typically constructed underground in soft, often sandy soil, with burrows that can extend up to 20 times the length of their bodies. These bees are frequently found nesting in coastal sand dunes and, on the Hebridean islands, in machair, which is a type of coastal grassland. In terms of appearance, Northern Colletes bees are medium-sized, measuring approximately 8–15 mm in length from head to body, and have a slender build. Their abdomens are black and feature narrow white bands on each segment. The thorax is covered with tawny-colored hairs, while the facial hairs are somewhat paler. They closely resemble other species within the Colletes genus, and when multiple Colletes species share the same habitat, microscopic examination may be required to differentiate between them. Female Northern Colletes are slightly larger than males, with longer, darker, and glossier abdomens. The life cycle of Northern Colletes begins with the emergence of adult bees in late June. They remain active until late August, but only during warm temperatures. Males typically emerge one or two days before females, and mating likely occurs shortly after the females emerge. After mating, the males die, while the females construct burrows that can reach depths of up to 26 cm. The females secrete a substance from glands in their mouths to create a cellophane-like lining for the burrow. Each egg is placed in an individual cell within the burrow, along with a supply of regurgitated nectar and pollen sufficient to sustain the larva through the winter. The larva develops underground, pupates within the burrow, and emerges as an adult the following June. Since Northern Colletes do not form colonies, there are no worker bees in this species. Northern Colletes is considered a rare species. In the British Isles, it nests along the Atlantic coasts of Ireland and northern England, as well as in coastal areas and islands of Scotland. In Northern Europe, it is found in low densities in coastal regions of Scandinavia. The species prefers south-facing slopes with sparse, low vegetation and forages in nearby flower-rich areas. In Southern Europe, however, it inhabits higher altitudes, such as the Pyrenees, Carpathians, and Altay Mountains. One of the most significant habitats for this species is the machair of the Outer Hebrides in Scotland. In September 2007, eleven previously unknown colonies of Northern Colletes were discovered in this region.
